profiles.Summary: Fallout: New Vegas runs well on the Steam Deck under Proton, earning a gold/trending-platinum ProtonDB rating — it is a 2010 Gamebryo engine title well within the Deck's capabilities and can hold 60 fps at native resolution with modest power draw. The main caveats are partial controller support requiring occasional touchpad use and engine-level CPU bottlenecks in dense areas like the New Vegas Strip.
profiles.BasisNote: No specific Steam Deck player reports were found; profiles are estimated from the game's 2010 PC minimum requirements (well below Deck capability), its Gamebryo engine characteristics, and the strong gold/trending-platinum ProtonDB rating — check frame pacing on the New Vegas Strip on your first run and reduce Shadow Distance if dips occur.

MaxBattery.Notes: Refresh rate locked to 30 Hz with a matching frame cap and a very low TDP squeezes maximum session length from the 40 Wh battery. FSR upscales from 960x600 acceptably for a 2010-era title; lower Object Fade and Actor Fade first if any stutters appear.

KnownIssues: Partial controller support — some menus and UI elements require touchpad or touchscreen input to navigate.
The Gamebryo engine is largely single-threaded, causing CPU-bound frame drops in dense areas such as the New Vegas Strip.
Occasional crashes on launch or mid-session have been reported; switching Proton versions (e.g. to Proton Experimental) can help.
Audio crackling or missing audio has been reported under some Proton versions; Proton Experimental generally resolves this.

MaxPerformance.Notes: New Vegas is CPU-bound in dense areas due to the single-threaded Gamebryo engine, so expect occasional dips on the New Vegas Strip even at full TDP; drop Shadow Distance to Medium if dips are frequent.

Optimal.Notes: Native 1280x800 with high settings runs well within the Deck's capabilities for this older engine; 60 fps holds steadily in most areas with the occasional dip in dense outdoor zones. This is the sweet spot for visual quality and battery life.

MaxBattery.Notes: At 5 W TDP and a low render resolution with FSR upscaling, the Deck sips power while keeping New Vegas perfectly playable. The 2010 engine is light enough that even these conservative settings look clean on the OLED screen.
